deliverables.text: A dimensioned, labeled diagram of each enclosure option — Project Horn's cone frustum and Project Orb's sphere — with the 3-D shape of each correctly named and every dimension used in the calculations marked directly on the diagram.
A materials-cost table showing each option's total exterior surface area and the resulting material cost per unit.
A packing-and-shipping table showing each option's packing efficiency inside a standard shipping container, units per container, and shipping cost per unit.

A total-cost-per-unit comparison table combining materials (D2), amortized mold tooling, and shipping (D3) for Project Horn vs. Project Orb at the client's target production volume, with a stated recommendation.

balance.argument_a: Project Horn's shipping-cost-per-unit is genuinely lower than Project Orb's ($0.1406 vs. $0.1868/unit at the 80% vs. 74.05% packing efficiencies in Appendix C) because a frustum nests far more efficiently than a sphere ever can. That real advantage just isn't quite large enough on its own at the 250,000-unit target volume: Horn's $0.232/unit amortized tooling (on a $58,000 mold) and $0.4895/unit material cost (157.90 sq in of shell) together outweigh the shipping edge, leaving Horn at $0.8621/unit total versus Orb's $0.7920/unit. Horn is also the shape the client's own audio engineer requires for acoustic dispersion performance, a real, non-cost argument that stands on its own.
balance.argument_b: Project Orb wins on total cost per unit, $0.7920 vs. Project Horn's $0.8621 — an 8.85% margin. The sphere's simpler mold ($32,000 vs. $58,000, or $0.128 vs. $0.232/unit amortized) and smaller shell surface area (153.94 sq in vs. 157.90 sq in, $0.4772 vs. $0.4895/unit material) both save real money on every one of the 250,000 units in the target run, and those savings outweigh the sphere's real but bounded shipping penalty — even though a sphere can never exceed roughly 74% packing density in a container (the Kepler-conjecture ceiling, $0.1868/unit shipping vs. Horn's $0.1406/unit). Orb is also the shape the studio's own creative director wants for shelf appeal.
balance.margin_basis: Total cost per unit for each option = (surface area x material cost per sq in) + (mold tooling cost / target production volume) + (freight cost per container / (container volume x packing efficiency / unit volume)), then compare Project Horn's and Project Orb's total cost per unit and express the gap as a percentage of the lower figure.
balance.computation_2026_08_27: Horn: surface area 157.90 sq in (closed frustum: lateral pi(R+r)l=106.84 + base pi*R^2=38.48 + top pi*r^2=12.57) x $0.0031/sq in = $0.4895 material; $58,000 tooling / 250,000 units = $0.2320; frustum volume (pi*h/3)(R^2+Rr+r^2)=146.08 cu in = 0.0845 cu ft, so 2,683 cu ft x 80% / 0.0845 cu ft = 25,391 units/container, $3,570.80 / 25,391 = $0.1406 shipping; total = $0.8621/unit. Orb: surface area 4*pi*r^2=153.94 sq in x $0.0031/sq in = $0.4772 material; $32,000 / 250,000 = $0.1280 tooling; sphere volume (4/3)*pi*r^3=179.59 cu in = 0.1039 cu ft, so 2,683 cu ft x 74.05% / 0.1039 cu ft = 19,117 units/container, $3,570.80 / 19,117 = $0.1868 shipping; total = $0.7920/unit. Gap = $0.0701, margin_pct = 0.0701/0.7920 = 8.85% -- Project Orb (B) wins by 8.85%, within SPEC Section 2's ~20% cap. RECOMPUTED 2026-08-27 (P6 remediation pass) after re-sourcing S3 (resin price $0.83->$0.88/lb) and S4 (density 0.0379->0.038 lb/in3); prior figure was 9.11%. Winner and qualitative shape of the case are unchanged. Computed honestly from the on-file MA1/MA2/MA4/MA6 assumptions and the freshly re-sourced S1/S2/S6 figures; no new figures invented.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Project Horn frustum dimensions (base radius, top radius, height) and Project Orb sphere radius
modeling_assumptions.value_used: Base 3.5 in, top 2.0 in, height 6.0 in, slant height 6.19 in (derived); sphere radius 3.5 in
modeling_assumptions.basis: No real spec exists for a fictional client's fictional prototype; sized to a plausible portable-Bluetooth-speaker footprint, sphere radius matched to the frustum's base radius so both shells plausibly house the same driver/battery stack.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: CORRECTED 2026-08-27 (P5 remediation -- the prior claim here was wrong): drives every downstream surface-area and volume figure for both options. A mechanical +/-50% flex of each of the four dimensions individually (cases/enclosure-call/sensitivity_model.py, run via tier2_probes.py --probe 5) shows this assumption CAN by itself flip the recommendation to Project Horn -- horn_base_r_in, horn_top_r_in, and horn_height_in each flip it at -50%, and orb_r_in flips it at +50% -- and several of the eight flex rows also breach SPEC Section 2's 20% balance cap even where the winner does not change. This is genuine geometry fragility, not a modeling artifact; see case.json.sensitivity_disclosure[] (Category F, one entry per dimension) for the full disclosure.

modeling_assumptions.basis: Plausible year-one volume for a mid-market consumer portable-audio SKU launch; no real client exists to source a number from.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Sets the amortized-tooling-cost-per-unit term. Below ~50,000 units/year, Project Horn's $26,000 tooling premium (MA6) can flip the recommendation toward Project Orb; above ~500,000 units/year the tooling gap becomes negligible per unit and the fixed packing-efficiency gap (MA4 vs. the 74.05% Kepler ceiling) dominates, favoring Project Horn more strongly. Confirmed stable under a mechanical +/-50% flex (does not flip the verdict or breach the 20% cap).

modeling_assumptions.basis: PC/ABS is a well-established material for consumer-electronics/speaker enclosures (S9); which material this fictional studio specifically chose is a scenario detail, not a fact to look up. Same material assumed for both shells so the comparison is not biased.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: None — identical for both options, cancels out of the Horn-vs-Orb comparison.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Project Horn packing efficiency inside a shipping container
modeling_assumptions.basis: Placed between the sphere's proven 74.05% Kepler ceiling and the 75-85% fill-rate guidance published for optimized rectangular cartons (S8, re-verified 2026-08-27) — a frustum nests better than a sphere (it can alternate orientation like stacked cups) but not as well as a true rectangular box.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The single most dilemma-sensitive assumption in the case. Near 75% (S8's re-verified lower-concern threshold) Project Horn's shipping advantage narrows sharply and the recommendation may flip toward Project Orb; near 85% (S8's 'achievable' upper figure) Project Horn's advantage widens. A mechanical +/-50% flex confirms this does NOT by itself flip the verdict (matching the original claim), but it does breach the SPEC Section 2 20% cap at -50% without flipping -- disclosed in case.json.sensitivity_disclosure[] (Category X).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Wall thickness used to derive material cost per sq in (feeds S6)
modeling_assumptions.basis: Midpoint of Protolabs' published recommended ABS wall-thickness range, 0.045-0.140 in (S5); no single published point value exists since wall thickness is a part-specific design choice.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Low — material cost is well under $1/unit next to amortized tooling and shipping, so this pick does not meaningfully affect the recommendation. Confirmed stable under a mechanical +/-50% flex.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Mold tooling cost (production-grade steel tooling at the MA2 volume)
modeling_assumptions.basis: Both anchored inside the published high-volume steel-tooling range of $5,000-$100,000 (S7, re-verified 2026-08-27); tapered geometry priced toward the top half per DFM guidance that added complexity (draft, taper, side-action risk) raises tooling cost, simple sphere priced toward the lower-middle. No public source gives a controlled dollar comparison between a tapered and a spherical mold for the same part.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: CORRECTED 2026-08-27 (P5 remediation): the $26,000 gap is $0.104/unit at the MA2 volume of 250,000 units — small next to the packing-efficiency gap (MA4), and a mechanical +/-50% flex confirms this is genuinely dilemma-sensitive on Project Horn's side alone: cutting Horn's own tooling cost by 50% (to $29,000) is, by itself, enough to flip the recommendation to Project Horn, and raising it by 50% (to $87,000) breaches the SPEC Section 2 20% cap in Project Orb's favor without flipping. (Project Orb's tooling cost is stable under the same +/-50% flex.) Disclosed in case.json.sensitivity_disclosure[] (Category X).

sensitivity_note: Three groups of assumptions are dilemma-flipping if disputed, confirmed by a mechanical +/-50% flex (cases/enclosure-call/sensitivity_model.py, P5): MA1's four geometry dials (horn_base_r_in, horn_top_r_in, horn_height_in, orb_r_in) can each independently flip the recommendation to Project Horn; MA6's horn_tooling_cost_usd alone can flip it the same way; and MA4 (Project Horn's packing efficiency, 80%, vs. the Kepler-proven 74.05% ceiling for Project Orb), while it does not flip the verdict by itself, breaches the SPEC Section 2 20% cap at its low end. At lower production volumes, MA2 (target production volume) interacting with MA6 also matters. A Hero who argues for different values on any of these should expect the recommendation, or at least the margin, to change; full disclosure with category and justification for every mechanically-unstable dial is recorded in sensitivity_disclosure[] below.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: No real client or prototype exists for Project Horn; the studio's foam-model base radius is a fictional scenario dimension with no real value that any amount of research could ever recover, and a mechanical -50% flex (to 1.75 in) flips the recommendation to Project Horn -- a genuine, disclosed instability, not a script defect.

Same fictional-prototype reasoning as horn_base_r_in: no real spec exists to source. A mechanical -50% flex (to 1.0 in) flips the recommendation to Project Horn, and +50% breaches the SPEC Section 2 20% cap without flipping.

Same fictional-prototype reasoning as horn_base_r_in: no real spec exists to source. A mechanical -50% flex (to 3.0 in) flips the recommendation to Project Horn and breaches the 20% cap; +50% also breaches the cap without flipping.

Same fictional-prototype reasoning as horn_base_r_in: no real spec exists to source Project Orb's sphere radius. A mechanical +50% flex (to 5.25 in) flips the recommendation to Project Horn, and -50% breaches the 20% cap without flipping.

MA4's true real-world value is knowable in principle (it could be measured by actually packing real frustum-shaped units into a real container) but is not publicly accessible for this fictional part; the case's 80% is a documented good-faith estimate placed between two public analogues (the Kepler 74.05% sphere-packing ceiling and S8's 75-85% rectangular-carton fill-rate guidance). A mechanical -50% flex (to 40%) breaches the SPEC Section 2 20% cap without flipping the verdict.

MA6's true tooling quote is knowable in principle (a real mold shop could quote it) but is not publicly accessible for this fictional part; $58,000 is a documented good-faith estimate anchored inside S7's published steel-tooling benchmark range and priced toward the top half per cited DFM complexity guidance. A mechanical -50% flex (to $29,000) is, by itself, enough to flip the recommendation to Project Horn.

derived.note_2026_08_27: material_cost_per_unit, total_cost_per_unit, margin_pct, and the twist figures were recomputed after re-sourcing S3 (resin price) and S4 (density) for P6; material cost per sq in moved from $0.0029 to $0.0031, margin_pct from 9.11% to 8.85%. Winner (B/Orb) and the twist's flip to A/Horn are unchanged.

cohort_bands.typical_size: 16-24 (the size this case was authored for)
cohort_bands.note: The full 45-minute Socratic plan and Anchor timings in FACILITATOR.md run as written; Anchors 2 and 3 run as separate passes, and the deep-conflict block (20:00-30:00) runs all three threads (acoustic-vs-cost, tooling-vs-shipping, Kepler-ceiling reliability).

Anchors 2 and 3 combine into a single 'what are we even deciding, and how' pass. The Twist still drops at the 15-minute mark, but the deep-conflict block drops to one thread (tooling-vs-shipping, the one the numbers most directly support) instead of three. Total runtime shortens proportionally; content is not cut.

There is no room to vote, so Anchor 1 becomes a stated initial position instead of a stand/sit vote. The facilitator plays devil's advocate directly rather than cold-calling other students. The Twist still lands as new information, but the Close's 'who reverses' becomes 'would you reverse, and why' addressed straight to the learner(s).

The +/-50% flex range itself was reviewed and judged reasonable for a fictional consumer-speaker enclosure (e.g. base radius 1.75-5.25in, height 3-9in) -- not widened or narrowed. All 9 sources[] URLs were freshly fetched and verified on 2026-08-27 (S1/S2/S5/S9 unchanged and reconfirmed live; S3/S4/S6/S7/S8 re-sourced/re-verified as above) -- see RESEARCH_LOG.md for the full fetch record. Re-sourcing S3/S4 changed the derived material-cost-per-sq-in from $0.0029 to $0.0031/in2, which moved margin_pct from 9.11% to 8.85% (still comfortably inside SPEC Section 2's 20% cap; winner unchanged, B/Project Orb) -- case.json.balance, case.json.derived, case.md, and FACILITATOR.md were all updated to the new figures so no document is left teaching a stale number. P1 cold-solve: PASS -- ran a genuinely fresh subagent (no access to FACILITATOR.md/case.json/QA_REPORT.md) against the current student packet; it independently reached B (Orb) with correct arithmetic matching the updated $0.862/$0.792-per-unit figures, correctly named the metric, and named MA1 (not MA4) as its most-sensitivity assumption -- a reasonable independent read now that MA1's disclosed instability is more prominent in the text, and not a contradiction of MA4 still being the single largest-swing individual dial. P3 trap-check: PASS -- the guide's named trap (stopping at the tooling-cost line without opening the shipping appendix) matches the fresh cold-solver's independent answer to 'least-supported number' (MA6's tooling-cost gap), same as the prior run. P4 twist-integrity: PASS -- twist logic and structure are unchanged (still independent of every stated Modeling Assumption); the illustrative twist margin moved from 13.32% to 12.75% toward Horn along with the base-margin recompute, still a genuine flip that does not make either option obviously correct. --- History: this case reached TIER1_PASS with P1-P4 PASS / P5-P6 NOT RUN on 2026-08-27 (first remediation pass), then P5/P6 were run for the first time and both genuinely FAILED (P5: MA1's own sensitivity claim was factually wrong -- flexing its 4 geometry dials and MA6's Horn tooling cost DOES flip the recommendation in several of 18 flex rows and breaches the 20% cap in 9; P6: S3/S6/S7/S8 had decayed and S4 was blocked) -- full detail on that run preserved in QA_REPORT.md. This pass closed both findings via disclosure+correction (P5) and re-sourcing (P6), per instruction not to fabricate a PASS and not to silently retune the geometry.
